newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FEATURE - Swiss hotdog seller loses battle with bureaucracy.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Swiss hotdog seller loses battle with bureaucracy.

text.p: Swiss hot dog seller Helmut Gerner has staged his last stand in the bureaucratically mean streets of Zurich, giving away hot dogs to protest rules he says led to the end of his business.
Gerner, 39, has fallen foul of the local office which licences Swiss businesses, the "Gewerbepolizei" (commercial police).
The business climate in Switzerland is distinctly chilly, economists say, and not just for hot dogs.
Gross domestic product (GDP) fell 0.7 percent in 1996 and is expected to grow by only about 0.5 percent in 1997.
Swiss GDP is the lowest of all 29 countries surveyed by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD).
ECONOMISTS SAY SMALL BUSINESS OVERREGULATED

Swiss economists blame the country's economic doldrums to a large degree on structural problems including overcapacity in key sectors like construction. But some say encouraging small business could provide a needed boost to the economy.

"One always tends to look at the large companies, but economies are made up of a big number of small and local companies," said Walter Diggelmann, executive director of the Swiss-American Chamber of Commerce.
"We certainly do have over-regulation in the area of small consumer businesses. There is still a very dense regulatory network and an opening up is badly needed," he added.
Some economists say there is also a problem of lack of ready credit, as big commercial banks pull back from lending to small businesses after losing money in bad loans in recent years.
Creditreform, which compiles data on the creditworthiness of borrowers, said that one sign of the trend was a drop in the number of new businesses with capital of over 500,000 francs ($340,000).
The problem may be partly that big banks are unable or unwilling to differentiate between different types of lending.
"For many years money has been easily available in Switzerland. Now, based on some hard experience, the banks are forced to take a closer look at the risk factor," said Diggelmann.
"We have to develop a culture to distinguish between a loan and entrepreneurial capital. There has been too much a mix in the past."
TOO MUCH PAPERWORK, TOO MANY TAXES
Swiss politicians are keen to improve chances for small and middle-sized companies, which they say are burdened by paperwork, taxes and other obstacles.
One study found small companies spend up to one full day a week on administrative chores.
Gerner said his initial investment involved buying 15 hot dog carts from Creative Mobile Systems in Manchester, Connecticut.
He was encouraged by findings from a Lucerne-based consultancy called Katag. Its deputy director, Michael Hostmann, says the "entire gastronomic business is in flux" as the Swiss eat more snacks.
But the Gewerbepolizei, responsible for issuing permits, could give Gerner only a permit for one cart.
He got initial approval to sell snacks, but then changed the name of his "substitute manager" and needed a new permit.
On April 24 he was re-issued a permit. This time it was only for sandwiches, sweets, fruits and non-alcoholic drinks. The permit omitted the word "snack."
NO "SNACK", NO SALES
"To me, a hot dog is a snack," said Gerner, who said that without the word on the permit he was not technically permitted to sell hot dogs.
In a letter to Reuters, the Gewerbepolizei denied Gerner had requested permission to sell hot dogs per se, and also cited doubts that he could keep food properly warm.
Gerner still cannot understand why the key word was omitted from his new permit. He also says hot dogs are supposed to be kept chilled until cooked with steam just before serving.
Tommaso Giordano, successful owner of Speedy Pizzaland, in Reinach, in the canton of Aargau, says good contacts are key to complying with local regulators.
"If someone wants something as a small business, it is tough. One needs good connections," he said.
Business here also is complicated by various laws governing shopping and dining hours in different Swiss communities.

Gerner was required to close shop at his one-man stall when Zurich stores close at 6:30 p.m., except for Thursdays when opening hours are longer. Thus he missed peak evening snacking time. On Saturdays, he had to close by 4 p.m. and on Sundays he could open for a maximum of five hours.
VENDORS PROTEST RESTRICTIONS
Some Zurich vendors recently demonstrated against restrictive hours in front of Zurich's city hall.
In the meantime, 23 shops in Zurich train station, which had been allowed to stay open longer hours, are being forced to close following a Federal Court ruling, resulting in some loss of jobs.
Bruno Kistler, spokesman for the Zurich police, denies the city is unfriendly to business, saying it had no choice but to apply the laws.
He also said city authorities were considering new rules to let stores stay open an extra hour and a half.
Meanwhile, Gerner has given up, saying he no longer has stomach for the fight.

He says that instead of employing people he will go on the dole himself, swelling the ranks of unemployed in a country where the jobless rate peaked at 5.7 percent, its highest level since the 1930s, earlier this year.
He also complains he was fined by authorities after he staged his hot dog give-away protest.
"I am being treated like a criminal," he said.
